results.question: What does the document say about methods?
results.answer: The document says that the request method token is the primary source of request semantics, indicating the purpose of the request and what the client expects as a successful result; its semantics might be further specialized by header fields if they do not conflict [p.72]. The method token is case-sensitive, since it might be used as a gateway to object-based systems with case-sensitive method names, and by convention standardized methods are defined in all-uppercase US-ASCII letters [p.73]. Unlike distributed objects, standardized request methods in HTTP are not resource-specific, because uniform interfaces provide better visibility and reuse in network-based systems; once defined, a standardized method ought to have the same semantics when applied to any resource, though each resource determines whether those semantics are implemented or allowed [p.73]. The document defines a number of standardized methods commonly used in HTTP [p.73], and states that all general-purpose servers MUST support GET and HEAD, while all other methods are OPTIONAL [p.74]. The set of methods allowed by a target resource can be listed in an Allow header field, though this set can change dynamically; an origin server receiving an unrecognized or unimplemented method SHOULD respond with 501 (Not Implemented), and one receiving a recognized and implemented but not allowed method SHOULD respond with 405 (Method Not Allowed) [p.74]. Additional methods outside the scope of the specification have been specified for use in HTTP and ought to be registered within the "Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Method Registry" [p.74]. Standardized methods are generic, potentially applicable to any resource, so new methods are preferably registered in a document not specific to a single application or data format [p.155]. Since message parsing needs to be independent of method semantics (aside from responses to HEAD), definitions of new methods cannot change the parsing algorithm or prohibit content on either the request or response message; they can specify only zero-length content by requiring a Content-Length header field with a value of "0", and cannot use the special host:port and asterisk forms of request target allowed for CONNECT and OPTIONS respectively, since a full URI in absolute form is needed [p.155].
